questions.question: What is a budget?
options: A plan that shows how much money we have and what we want to use it for
A list of random numbers that only parents write
A list of things we want to buy with pocket money. Only kids ever have one
A drawing notebook
questions.explanation: A budget is a plan for your money – it helps keep it in order.

questions.question: Chrumko sees that mom is writing numbers in a notebook. What is she doing?
options: Doing the homework Chrumko got at school.
Planning expenses for the whole month
Writing a story, because she wants to become a writer
Drawing pictures that Chrumko can color in
questions.explanation: Mom first writes down the money the family will receive, then what needs to be paid.

questions.question: A budget shows only what we spend, not what we receive.
questions.explanation: A budget shows both income and expenses, and the balance.

questions.question: One of these statements is wrong. Find it.
options: A budget shows income and expenses.
A budget helps keep money in order.
A budget is useless and nobody needs it.
questions.explanation: A budget is a plan for money that keeps us in control.

questions.question: Match each term with its meaning.
matchRight: Money that comes in
Money that goes out
A plan for your money
What is left after subtracting expenses from income
questions.explanation: A budget consists of income, expenses and balance.

questions.question: Sort the items into income or expenses.
questions.explanation: Income is money that comes in, expenses are money that goes out.

questions.question: Put the steps of how mom plans a budget in order.
orderItems: Mom writes down the money the family will receive
Mom writes down what needs to be paid
Mom finds out what is left
questions.explanation: Budgeting follows a logical process.

questions.question: Why is a budget important?
options: It keeps you in control, instead of constantly wondering 'where did it all go?'
It is just a list of phone numbers
All the numbers are random, so it is completely useless
A budget tells how many sweets Chrumko has had today
questions.explanation: A budget is a plan for your money.

questions.question: What are income and what are expenses?
options: Income is money that goes out; expenses are money that comes in
There is no difference between them
Income is debt, expenses are savings
Income is money that comes in; expenses are money that goes out
questions.explanation: You need to watch both sides – what comes in and what goes out.

questions.question: Chrumko thinks that when parents get paid, they can buy everything right away. What does dad show him?
options: That they will really buy everything, because money is endless
That nothing gets used up, even if they buy everything
First you need to subtract housing, food and other bills
That everything is free
questions.explanation: After paying the expenses, a smaller amount is left.

questions.question: If income is higher than expenses, you can save the difference.
questions.explanation: If income > expenses, the difference can be saved.

questions.question: One of these statements is wrong. Find it.
options: Income and expenses are always the same.
If expenses > income, we spend more than we earn.
A healthy budget keeps expenses below income.
questions.explanation: Income and expenses differ – that's why you need to track both.

questions.question: Match each situation with its meaning.
matchRight: You spend more than you earn – a problem
Expenses stay below income
Money that comes in
You can save the difference
questions.explanation: The relationship between income and expenses decides whether you can save.

questions.question: Sort the situations by whether you can save or have a problem.
dragTargets: You spend more than you earn
questions.explanation: If income > expenses, you can save. If expenses > income, it's a problem.

questions.question: What does Chrumko realize about income and expenses?
options: Money is pointless, because you always end up in the red
What matters is not only what comes in, but also what goes out
Everything is free, so income and expenses don't matter
You don't need to track expenses, it's enough to track income
questions.explanation: You need to watch both sides: what comes in and what goes out.

questions.question: Why doesn't the family spend all the money at the beginning of the month?
options: For no reason
It always gets spent right at the beginning of the month
Money multiplies by itself during the month
The money has to last the whole month
questions.explanation: A month has 30 days and the money has to last all 30.

questions.question: Chrumko suggests buying a new game right after payday. What does mom say?
options: Yes, they'll buy it right away, because everyone wants it
The game is more important than everything else, so they must buy it right away
First you need to pay everything important, only then will they see what they can afford extra
They won't buy anything without discussion
questions.explanation: In a few days, more payments for school and the household will come.

questions.question: Money should be spread over the whole month, not just the first few days.
questions.explanation: Spreading money out is the key to having enough throughout the whole month.

questions.question: One of these statements is wrong. Find it.
options: Money has to last all 30 days of the month.
First you need to pay everything important.
After payday you should immediately buy everything we want.
questions.explanation: Money should be spread over the whole month.

questions.question: Match each planning step with its description.
matchRight: Know your monthly income
List all regular expenses
It has 30 days – the money has to last all of them
What's left is for other expenses and saving
questions.explanation: Monthly planning has clear steps.

questions.question: Sort the activities by whether they come first or later.
questions.explanation: Important things are paid first, only then whatever is left.

questions.question: Put the steps of monthly planning in order.
orderItems: Use the balance for other expenses and saving
questions.explanation: The logical process of monthly planning.

questions.question: What are fixed expenses?
options: Payments that repeat regularly in the same amount
Expenses that change every day
Expenses paid only once in a lifetime
Purchases the family makes up
questions.explanation: Fixed expenses are payments that always repeat the same, for example rent or internet.

questions.question: Chrumko asks why his parents talk about the same payments every month. What does dad show him?
options: That there are no bills, in reality they pay for new computer games every month
The internet and rent bills, which come regularly
That payments change every day and nobody knows why
That everything is free
questions.explanation: These payments stay the same, even when the family buys nothing new.

questions.question: We can skip fixed expenses in the budget if we don't want to pay.
questions.explanation: You can't skip fixed expenses, so you count them in first.

questions.question: One of these statements is wrong. Find it.
options: We can skip fixed expenses if we don't feel like paying.
Fixed expenses repeat regularly.
Rent is an example of a fixed expense.
questions.explanation: You can't skip fixed expenses.

questions.question: Match each term with its description.
matchRight: The same amount every month
They come first in the budget
Regular monthly subscription
An important cost so Chrumko isn't hungry
questions.explanation: Fixed expenses are regular and predictable.

questions.question: Sort the items by whether they repeat the same every month.
questions.explanation: Fixed expenses stay the same, even when the family buys nothing new.

questions.question: Why are fixed expenses important in a budget?
options: They change every day, so we should write them down every day
They aren't important, only expenses for toys and sweets are
They are paid only once a year
They come first and we can't skip them, so we count them in
questions.explanation: Fixed expenses come first in every budget.

questions.question: What are variable expenses?
options: Expenses that never change
Expenses that are always the same
Expenses that change according to need
Expenses that don't exist
questions.explanation: Sometimes they are higher, sometimes lower.

questions.question: One week Chrumko buys only basic groceries. Another week they also buy extra fruit, school supplies and a gift for grandma. What happens?
options: The amount at the checkout is higher
The amount is the same, because the amount depends on the time of shopping
Everything is free
The family buys nothing in order to save
questions.explanation: Some expenses change depending on what is needed.

questions.question: Variable expenses change depending on what is needed at the moment.
questions.explanation: That's why a good budget has room for surprises.

questions.question: One of these statements is wrong. Find it.
options: Variable expenses change from month to month.
Variable expenses are always the same amount.
Variable expenses include groceries and clothing.
questions.explanation: Variable expenses differ – that's their nature.

questions.question: Match each expense with its description.
matchRight: Leave a flexible amount for them in the budget
Bought only if what we have at home gets damaged
They differ during the year, e.g. on holidays, at birthdays
Quantities and kinds change every week
questions.explanation: Variable expenses are unpredictable, but we can plan for them.

questions.question: Sort the variable expenses into the correct groups.
questions.explanation: Food, clothing and events all belong among expenses that change.

questions.question: What does Chrumko realize about expenses?
options: All months cost exactly the same
Expenses don't exist, because everything is free
Everything is chaotic
Not every month costs exactly the same
questions.explanation: Some expenses change, so you need to leave a flexible amount in the budget.
